Name: Designating July 11th annually as Lil’ Kim Day.
Title: Resolution designating July 11th annually as Lil’ Kim Day in the City of New York to honor her as a pioneer of women in the rap genre and an influential musical artist born and raised in Brooklyn, New York.
BodyName: Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries and International Relations

History.Description: This Resolution was Introduced by Council
This Resolution was Referred to Comm by Council to the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries and International Relations
History.AgendaNote: Cultural Affairs, Libraries and International Relations

Text:
Whereas, Kimberly Denise Jones was born on July 11, 1974, in the Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York, with her mother, father, and brother; and
Whereas, When Kim’s father became physically abusive toward his wife, Kim, her mother, and brother moved to New Rochelle, New York, to escape the violence and later moved back to the City with her father due to custody arrangements; and
Whereas, As Kim grew older, she faced both physical and verbal abuse from her father, and at 14 years old, she left home; and
Whereas, In 1993, on the streets of Brooklyn, Kim met Christopher Wallace, also known as “Biggie Smalls,” and impressed him with her freestyle rap; and
Whereas, Biggie championed Kim and used his relationship with Bad Boy Records, a hip-hop record label founded by Sean “Diddy” Combs, to recruit her to join the rap group Junior M.A.F.I.A.; and
Whereas, It was the success of the songs “Player’s Anthem” and “Get Money” on the Conspiracy album, debuted in 1995, that launched Kim’s career as “Lil’ Kim,” the only female artist in the group; and
Whereas, With Biggie as her executive producer, Lil’ Kim’s 1996 solo album, “Hard Core,” in 1996 debuted at No. 11 on the Billboard 100 album chart, making it an instant hit; and
Whereas, Lil’ Kim’s unapologetic sex positivity, blonde wigs, and blue contact lenses turned heads in the music industry and contributed to her unique style; and
Whereas, Lil’ Kim appealed to audiences through cover art with revealing and feminine outfits previously unknown to female rap artists; and
Whereas, Biggie continued to work with Lil’ Kim, developing her image as an artist, and the two maintained both a working and romantic relationship; and
Whereas, In 1997, Biggie was killed, and the loss deeply affected Lil’ Kim, causing her to pause her music career for three years; and
Whereas, Lil’ Kim’s second album, “The Notorious K.I.M.,” a tribute to the instrumental role Biggie played in her life and her career, reached No. 4 on the Billboard 200 chart in 2000; and
Whereas, In 2001, Lil’ Kim collaborated with Christina Aguilera, Pink, Mya, and Missy Elliot to remake Patti Labelle’s “Lady Marmalade” for the soundtrack of the movie, “Moulin Rouge”; and
Whereas, In 2002, “Lady Marmalade” won a Grammy Award for Best Pop Collaboration with Vocals and established Lil’ Kim as a voice in hip hop; and
Whereas, Lil’ Kim received a Grammy nomination for Best Female Rap Solo Performance for her song “Came Back for You” and Best Rap Collaboration for her song “Magic Stick;” and
Whereas, Lil’ Kim won two Source hip-hop music awards and won two awards in 2003, including “Female Hip-Hop Artist of the Year” and “Female Singer of the Year for her song, “The Jump Off”; and
Whereas, in 2004, Lil’ Kim created her own foundation called Lil’ Kim Cares to raise funds and awareness for national programs assisting those experiencing homelessness, HIV/AIDS, transitional living, children experiencing neglect, and women facing domestic violence; and
Whereas, With her rhymes, Lil’ Kim took the misogynistic sexuality of hardcore male rap and converted it into empowerment for female rappers; and
Whereas, Lil’ Kim’s lyrics challenged gender stereotypes and her provocative style broke barriers for future women in rap like Cardi B and Megan Thee Stallion; and
Whereas, Lil’ Kim’s bold music choices and groundbreaking imagery revolutionized rap, making her a part of the vibrant history of the genre born in New York City; now, therefore, be it
Resolved, That the Council of the City of New York designates July 11th annually as Lil’ Kim Day to honor her as a pioneer of women in the rap genre and an influential musical artist born and raised in Brooklyn, New York.
